title: Itch & xerosis in older adults
summary: Asteatotic eczema, venous and discoid eczema, lichen simplex and prurigo — with scabies and bullous pemphigoid as don’t-miss itch differentials.

glance.think: Dry, cracked “crazy-paving” shins or generalised itch in an older person, often worse in winter after hot baths and soaps.
glance.engine: Age-related barrier lipid loss plus environment, drugs and comorbidities drive xerosis → fissures → itch–scratch.
glance.backbone: Liberal greasy emollients and soap substitutes every day; short moderately potent steroid for asteatotic flares; review diuretics/statins with the GP.
glance.never_miss: Itch out of proportion to rash — think scabies, bullous pemphigoid, and systemic disease (CKD, cholestasis, lymphoma).

what: **Xerosis** (dry skin) is the commonest skin problem and the commonest cause of itch in older adults. **Asteatotic eczema** (eczema craquelé) is the inflammatory end — polygonal “crazy-paving” red fissures, typically on the shins.

This page also covers related elderly itch patterns: venous (stasis) eczema, discoid eczema, lichen simplex / nodular prurigo, and the red-flag differentials of [scabies](condition:scabies) and pre-bullous pemphigoid.

list: Ageing epidermis: fewer lipids and NMF, slower repair, higher water loss; less sebum/sweat.
Environment: low humidity, central heating, hot showers, soaps and antiseptic washes.
Drugs: diuretics, **statins**, retinoids, some antiandrogens, chemotherapy/EGFR inhibitors.
Systemic: hypothyroidism, CKD, diabetes, malnutrition, HIV, malignancy (acquired ichthyosis).
Dull rough scale, tight feel, nocturnal itch; winter flares.
Asteatotic eczema: shallow red fissures in a cracked-porcelain network on shins (± thighs, arms).
Venous eczema: medial gaiter area with haemosiderin, oedema, varicose veins — see also [venous leg ulcer](condition:venous-leg-ulcer) / [red leg](condition:red-leg).
Discoid eczema: coin-shaped weeping plaques.
Lichen simplex / prurigo: thick scratched plaques or nodules at reachable sites.

features.title: Skin of colour
features.text: Erythema may look violaceous or grey-brown; judge on scale, thickening and symptoms.

list: Clinical: season, bathing habits, products, drugs, care-home contacts.
Itch >> rash, new generalised dryness, or resistance → systemic screen and “don’t miss” list below.
Swab only if infected; patch test if products seem to worsen it.

head: Look-alike
Clues
rows: Burrows, nocturnal itch, itchy contacts/care home
Urticated plaques, intense itch, older adult → refer
Little rash; weight loss, night sweats, nodes

list: Emollients **liberally and often** (≥2–3× daily and after washing). Greasier ointments for legs; urea 5–10% for scale.
Soap substitutes; short lukewarm showers; pat dry; no bubble bath.
Humidify rooms; cotton clothes.
**Fire risk:** paraffin (and other) emollients on fabrics — no smoking/naked flames; wash clothing often (MHRA).
**Falls risk:** slippery bathroom floors — non-slip mats; apply after stepping out.
Asteatotic flare: short **moderately potent** topical steroid (e.g. clobetasone butyrate) 1–2 weeks plus ongoing emollient; potent short-term for thick leg plaques.
Infected eczema: treat per NICE guidance — avoid routine topical antibiotics.
Drug review with the GP (diuretic/statin) — do not stop cardiovascular drugs unilaterally.
Venous eczema: emollient + steroid + compression after ABPI assessment pathways.
Lichen simplex/prurigo: potent steroid ± occlusion; address itch driver; refer if refractory.

red_flags: Generalised itch with little rash, weight loss, night sweats or lymphadenopathy → systemic work-up.
Suspected scabies outbreak in a care home.
New intense itch with urticated plaques in an older adult → consider pemphigoid; refer.
Non-healing “eczema” → patch testing or alternative diagnosis.
pearls: “Steroid settles it but it always comes back” usually means **no maintenance emollient**.
Help older people reach their legs — carers, pumps, long-handled applicators.
Teach fingertip units; steroid treats the flare, emollient prevents the next one.
